summary:
Maine law prohibits discrimination on the basis of actual or perceived gender identity or expression in employment, housing, credit, public accommodations and education opportunity. The protections were added in 2005 and retained after a veto referendum on 8 November 2005, and LD 1688, signed on 17 June 2021, wrote gender identity explicitly into state statutes. The state hate-crime law provides penalty enhancements for offences motivated by actual or perceived gender identity, and the gay and trans panic defence was abolished by legislation passed in June 2019 by 132-1 in the House and 35-0 in the Senate, effective 1 July 2019.

Gender markers on Maine driver's licences and state identification cards can be changed without medical provider certification, a rule in place since November 2019, on a completed Gender Designation Form offering male, female and X options. Birth certificates reflecting gender identity, including an X marker, have been issued since July 2020 on notarized affidavit. The X marker on a birth certificate requires a declaration from a licensed physician or mental health provider, and applicants who are minors require parental consent.

Maine has no state law restricting transgender people's use of sex-segregated facilities. The Maine Supreme Court ruled in January 2014 in Doe v. Regional School Unit 26 against a school district that had denied a student use of the bathroom aligned with her gender identity.

A law effective since July 2023 allows 16 and 17 year olds to obtain hormone therapy as gender-affirming care, and an April 2024 law explicitly protects, defends and safeguards gender-affirming healthcare. From 1 October 2026 healthcare facilities in Maine must mandate and include sexual orientation and gender identity data.

In June 2025 the Maine Senate rejected Legislative Document 233, which would have barred transgender women from competing in women's sports in state-funded schools. It was the only one of eight anti-trans bills introduced in the state in 2025 to pass the House.

The University of Maine System announced on 21 March 2025, with an update on 24 March, that it would comply with federal restrictions on transgender sports participation. The announcement followed the US Department of Agriculture's suspension of federal funding for research and programmes while it investigated possible sex-based discrimination in federally funded education programmes.

A July 2026 national anti-trans legal risk assessment places Maine in its Low-Risk States group. The same assessment separately flags that Maine's risk has increased because of the University of Maine System's capitulation on sports participation.
tangentialFactors: Maine's civil-rights protections for sexual orientation, later extended explicitly to gender identity, have survived two repeal attempts by referendum. The Maine Human Rights Act, 5 M.R.S. §4551 et seq., was amended by PL 2005, c. 10 (LD 1196) to extend protections regardless of sexual orientation, after the 1997 protections (PL 1997, c. 205) were repealed in a people's veto on 10 February 1998 and the 1999 protections (PL 1999, c. 629) were defeated in a referendum on 7 November 2000. The 2005 protections survived the people's veto referendum of 8 November 2005.
localsOnly:
Maine Corrections houses Andrea Balcer, a 27-year-old transgender woman convicted of double murder, in the women's facility at the Maine Correctional Center in Windham, where she had been held for at least a year as of April 2026. The placement follows current gender identity rather than birth sex. On 3 April 2026 another inmate, Katie Mountain, 41, filed a 30-page complaint against MDOC Commissioner Randall Liberty, Warden Ben Beal and Balcer, alleging chronic harassment and assault by the transgender prisoner; the complaint was filed by attorney Cynthia Dill and no ruling has been reported. The harassment and assault claims are allegations; the placement of a transgender woman in the women's prison is documented.

Licensed health care providers in Maine are prohibited from practising conversion therapy on minors under legislation signed on 29 May 2019 and effective 17 September 2019. A 2018 ban bill passed both chambers but was vetoed on 6 July 2018, and the override failed 79-61 on 9 July 2018.

Maine Democrats voted unanimously in January 2024 to set aside a bill that would have provided sanctuary protections to transgender minors, following public backlash.
outOfScopeNotes:
The harassment and assault allegations in the April 2026 complaint against the corrections commissioner, the warden and the transgender prisoner are untested; no ruling had been reported at the time of the source.

The July 2026 assessment's criteria and methodology are not described in the source; its low-risk grouping and its increased-risk flag for Maine are reported as the assessment's conclusions.

Whether the University of Maine System's March 2025 compliance with federal sports restrictions remains in force is not established by the sources.

Whether the sanctuary bill for transgender minors has been reintroduced in a later legislative session is not sourced.

The inventory contains no Maine-specific figures on violence against transgender residents or visitors and no state-level enforcement statistics for the hate-crime enhancement.
